passage: Amara sat in her car outside the clinic in Nairobi for ten minutes before going in. For weeks she had been waking at four with her mind racing about work, then dragging through the day. Rafael, a colleague, had said gently, "Maybe talk to someone?" She had read symptom pages online, and every page gave a different explanation. She closed the tabs and booked an appointment instead. Inside, the doctor asked questions and listened, named nothing on the first day, and suggested a follow-up with a counsellor. Amara wrote down what was said and booked the second appointment at the desk. On the drive home she felt something like relief: unsure, but not alone. At a red light she texted Rafael: "I went."

qa.q: Where did Amara wait before going in to the appointment?
qa.a: She waited in her car outside the clinic in Nairobi.

qa.q: What was Amara feeling on the drive home?
qa.a: Amara felt relieved, unsure of what comes next but no longer alone.

qa.q: What could Amara do if the guidance feels hard to follow?
qa.a: Amara could tell the doctor or counsellor at the next appointment and ask for changes, rather than guessing or dropping it.

qa.q: How might Rafael have felt when the text arrived?
qa.a: Rafael may have felt glad and relieved that the gentle suggestion had been taken up.

grounding: Amara books an appointment to talk about how she feels and follows the doctor's guidance instead of self-diagnosing.

subtype: Approach: root cause analysis of the work drivers [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Zubin stared at his screen, too tired to type. Preeti, his wife, set a cup of tea beside him. "Why am I this exhausted?" he asked the room, as though the question were new. He started a list.

Wednesday. He wrote the reasons as they came: nobody had agreed this quarter's priorities, so everything felt urgent. No leave taken in eleven months. And he kept saying yes to jobs that belonged to other people. "A weekend off won't fix any of that," he told Preeti.

Saturday. He booked two leave days for next month, messaged his manager asking for the priorities to be ranked, and told a colleague he could no longer take on that colleague's reports. Preeti read over the list. "That's three things you can actually change," she said. Zubin nodded and slept until ten.

qa.q: How long had Zubin gone without taking leave?
qa.a: He had taken no leave in eleven months.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling on Monday?
qa.a: Zubin felt drained and worn out, too tired even to type.

qa.q: What else could Zubin do beyond the three changes?
qa.a: Zubin could ask the manager to share out some tasks, plan regular breaks, and see a doctor if the exhaustion does not ease.

qa.q: How might Preeti see Zubin's list?
qa.a: Preeti may feel hopeful and relieved, since the list gives three concrete things that can change.

grounding: Zubin asks why he is exhausted and names unclear priorities, no leave and taking on others' tasks, so he can change more than his rest.

subtype: Approach: taking planned leave and reducing load [Action]
passage:
'The vendor tracker and the newsletter,' said Minakshi, sliding the folder across. 'Those are the two I'm handing over. Everything's documented.'
'And you're really taking the full two weeks?' said Damini.
'I've got leave piled up from a year I never used. I'm using it.'
'What about when you're back?'
'I've asked our manager to cut my load for a month and bring the work back gradually. Half of what I did before, for the first two weeks.'
'Honestly? I was wondering when you'd stop.' Damini opened the folder. 'I'll cover them. Just make sure your phone isn't in your bag.'
'It's switched off.' Minakshi laughed, a small tired sound. 'I'm going to sleep for three days.'

qa.q: Which two projects did Minakshi hand over?
qa.a: The vendor tracker and the newsletter.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's small tired laugh suggest about how Minakshi feels?
qa.a: It suggests Minakshi is worn out but relieved to be stopping.

qa.q: What else could support Minakshi's return to work?
qa.a: Minakshi could have regular short check-ins with the manager and start with lighter meetings, adjusting the pace if energy dips.

qa.q: How might Damini feel about taking the projects?
qa.a: Damini seems willing and supportive, having wondered when Minakshi would stop, though the extra work may still be a lot.

grounding: Minakshi uses stored leave, hands over two projects and asks the manager for a lighter load and gradual restart.

subtype: Approach: rebuilding daily routines for sleep and movement [Action]
passage: My brother Lalit stayed with me for a few weeks last spring after a hard year at work, and I watched him build a routine. He chose a sleep time and stuck a note on the bathroom mirror: lights out at eleven. Every evening at seven he walked around the block for twenty minutes, whatever the weather, and after dinner he left his phone in the hall for an hour. He didn't announce a new life. He called it "the small things". I couldn't tell you whether he was happy. Some nights he was quiet at dinner. But by the third week he was up before me, and the walk had become something he did without being asked. He had dropped the idea of changing everything at once. - Kavitha

qa.q: How long was Lalit's evening walk?
qa.a: It was twenty minutes.

qa.q: What might Lalit have been feeling on the quiet nights at dinner?
qa.a: Kavitha cannot tell for sure, but Lalit might have been tired or low, since the quiet nights sat beside the routine.

qa.q: Why might small routines work better than a big overhaul, and what could Lalit do if he still feels worn out?
qa.a: Small routines are easier to keep up than a sweeping change; if Lalit still feels worn out, he could see a doctor or counsellor.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see the change in Lalit?
qa.a: Kavitha sees steady progress, such as being up early and walking unprompted, while admitting not knowing what Lalit feels inside.

grounding: Lalit sets a regular sleep time, a twenty-minute evening walk and a screen-free hour, small routines rather than an overhaul.

subtype: Approach: pushing through with more effort [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Pallavi,

You asked why I sounded so flat on the phone, so here it is. Since March I have been telling myself I only lack discipline. So I began work at five every morning and stopped taking lunch breaks. I skipped my Saturday football, because rest felt like an excuse. It has gone the other way. Last week I sent a client the wrong file, twice, and my manager said my last report was full of small mistakes I would never have made before. I am more tired than in March, not less. I can see now that more effort was the one thing that could not help. I am going to talk to my doctor this week and tell my manager honestly what is going on. I wanted you to hear it first.

Girish

qa.q: What did Girish give up while trying to be more disciplined?
qa.a: Girish gave up lunch breaks and Saturday football.

qa.q: How does Girish feel about the plan of simply pushing harder?
qa.a: Girish now sees it as a mistake and feels tired and worried.

qa.q: What could work better than pushing through?
qa.a: Girish could rest properly, talk to the doctor, and tell the manager so the workload can be looked at.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt hearing the flat voice, and then the letter?
qa.a: Pallavi may have felt worried about Girish, and glad to be told first.

grounding: Girish believes discipline alone will fix the exhaustion, adds early work and cuts rest, and the errors rise.

subtype: Approach: taking a holiday and returning to the same conditions [Pitfall]
passage: When Taniya came back from her week in Goa, she looked ten years younger: sun on her face, laughing, telling the whole floor about a sunrise swim. I sat two desks away and was glad for her. On Monday the same inbox was waiting, three meetings back to back, and a deadline that had crept forward while she was away. By the second week she was answering emails at ten at night again. By the fourth she had stopped laughing at lunch, was snapping at small things, and sometimes stared at the ceiling in the middle of meetings. I don't know what was going on in her head. I do know nothing at work had changed while she was away, and the holiday's glow faded fast. - Thomas

qa.q: Where did Taniya spend her week away?
qa.a: Taniya spent it in Goa.

qa.q: What might Taniya have been feeling by the fourth week?
qa.a: Thomas can only guess, but Taniya seemed strained and irritable, snapping at small things and staring at the ceiling in meetings.

qa.q: What could Taniya do differently after the next break?
qa.a: Taniya could ask the manager to change the workload and meeting load before or on return, and see a doctor if the tiredness comes back.

qa.q: How does Thomas explain why the holiday did not last?
qa.a: Thomas sees that nothing at work changed while Taniya was away, so the same pressure was waiting.

grounding: Taniya returns refreshed from a week away to the same workload and meetings, and the exhaustion returns within a month.

subtype: Approach: emotion-aware pacing of the return [Thinking]
passage: Vijay came back on a Monday in September after three months off, and I watched him do it carefully. He had told the team he would work half-days for the first week, and he kept to it: gone by one, no arguing. He asked for the heavy budget review to be moved to the following week. He had a ten-minute check-in with our manager on Thursday and wrote something in a small notebook afterwards. Once I saw him stop mid-sentence in a meeting, breathe, and say, "I need five minutes." He stepped out and came back steadier. I can't say what he felt in those moments. He looked a bit tense, a bit determined. But he treated his tiredness like a gauge on a dashboard, not something to shout down. - Anirban

qa.q: How long did Vijay work half-days after returning?
qa.a: Vijay worked half-days for the first week.

qa.q: What might Vijay have felt when he stopped mid-sentence and stepped out?
qa.a: Anirban cannot be sure, but Vijay looked tense and determined, as if listening to his own tiredness.

qa.q: What could Vijay do after the first week?
qa.a: Vijay could raise his hours in steps, keep the check-ins, and slow down again if his energy dips.

qa.q: How does Anirban see Vijay's return?
qa.a: Anirban sees it as careful and steady, with tiredness treated as a signal instead of something to ignore.

grounding: Vijay plans a gradual return with half-days, light early meetings and a manager check-in, and watches his energy as a signal.

subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan when relapse signs appear [Revision]
passage: Three weeks after Bidisha came back from her break, the deadlines came back too. I sit next to her, so I noticed things before she said anything: her laptop still open when I left, the untouched lunchbox, the dark circles returning. On a Tuesday she stood up and knocked on the manager's door. She came out ten minutes later, sat down, and told me quietly she had asked to drop the vendor review from her list. She had also added a weekly counselling session to her calendar, on Wednesday evenings. She did not seem ashamed. She said, "That's just information. It's telling me the plan needs changing." I'm not sure how she felt underneath. She looked tired, but lighter. - Vikas

qa.q: What did Bidisha drop from her list?
qa.a: Bidisha dropped the vendor review.

qa.q: What might Bidisha have felt about the signs coming back?
qa.a: Vikas is not sure, but Bidisha did not seem ashamed, and looked tired yet lighter, treating the signs as information.

qa.q: What else could help Bidisha keep watch over her recovery?
qa.a: Bidisha could check her sleep and workload each week, and talk to the counsellor or a doctor if things get worse.

qa.q: How does Vikas see Bidisha's response?
qa.a: Vikas noticed the early signs from the next desk and seems impressed by how calmly Bidisha acted.

grounding: Bidisha notices worsening sleep as deadlines return, tells her manager, drops a commitment and adds counselling, treating the relapse as information.

subtype: Approach: tracking every expense for two months [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday, week one. Omkar and Hafsa opened a shared budget app and promised to log every expense for two months, even the tea from the corner stall.

Sunday, week seven. Hafsa scrolled through the categories and read one out slowly. "Food delivery and subscriptions together. A fifth of what we earn." Omkar checked it. "That can't be right." It was. "I was sure it was the rent."

Sunday, week nine. They cancelled three subscriptions, set a limit of two delivery nights a month, and started cooking together on Wednesdays. "The surprise was the point," Omkar said. "I'd have argued about the rent for another year."

qa.q: What did Omkar and Hafsa promise to do for two months?
qa.a: They promised to log every expense in the shared app, even the tea from the corner stall.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when Hafsa read out the total?
qa.a: Omkar felt surprised and disbelieving, saying "That can't be right."

qa.q: What else could they try to keep spending on track?
qa.a: They could review the categories together each month and set a weekly amount for food, so surprises show up sooner.

qa.q: How might Hafsa have felt on finding the total?
qa.a: Hafsa may have felt startled but also curious, since Hafsa read the figure out slowly and then joined in checking it.

grounding: Omkar and Hafsa track all spending for two months and are surprised to find delivery and subscriptions take a fifth of their income.

subtype: Approach: category limits with a monthly plan [Action]
passage:
Deepika: Draft is done. Rent, groceries, transport, savings, fun. Numbers are in the sheet.
Asif: Fun is smaller than I'd like 😅
Deepika: It's what's left. Sit-down is on the 1st, remember.
(Later in the month)
Asif: Groceries are already gone?? It's only the 24th
Deepika: The party weekend. We ordered in too. Groceries ran out.
Asif: So do we take it from fun or from savings?
Deepika: Let's not decide alone. Tonight?
Asif: Tonight. I'll bring the sheet.
Deepika: 👍 My idea: move a bit from fun this month and leave savings alone.
Asif: Fair. Fun does not need to be big, just there.

qa.q: On which date is the monthly sit-down for Deepika and Asif?
qa.a: The sit-down is on the 1st.

qa.q: What does Asif's reaction to the size of the fun category suggest about how Asif feels?
qa.a: It suggests Asif feels mildly disappointed but good-humoured, since the reaction comes with a laughing face.

qa.q: What could they do to stop groceries running out early?
qa.a: They could check the grocery amount weekly and keep a small buffer, and plan party weekends into the sheet in advance.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel about groceries running out on the 24th?
qa.a: Deepika seems calm and steady, insisting that they decide together rather than one of them choosing alone.

grounding: Deepika and Asif give each category an amount, review on the first of the month, and decide together whether to shift funds when one runs out.
